translations.answer: The practitioner in the thread explains that humanoid robots with lower-level position control, such as iCub and Talos, typically use theoretical/virtual state information (TSID) in the model for open-loop calculation. The stabilizer (stabilizer) is then constructed using foot force/torque sensors and/or IMU, and the stabilizer modifies the TSID reference, for example, adjusting the center of mass (CoM) reference. He also mentions that an attempt was made to use a closed-loop floating base and maintain theoretical state information in the joints, but the complete conditions and results were not provided in the comments, so this part cannot be considered a definitive solution.
translations.applicability: Applicable to humanoid robots with lower-level position control, foot force/torque (F/T), or IMU. The stabilizer structure, reference correction, and gain adjustment must be individually designed for each robot.
translations.credibility.rationale: There is existing engineering records for the environment, processing steps, and results, but formal cross-validation or independent replication has not been conducted.
translations.details.attempts.0: The maintainer provides an open-loop TSID and control boundaries for QP. The practitioner shares the model state TSID with foot force/torque (F/T)/IMU stabilizer. The questioner attempts a real floating base, Cartesian end-effector error integration, contact reference, and gain adjustment.
translations.details.diagnostics.0: Distinguishes between the QP state used, integration start point, and feedback position of the lower-level position PID. Checks if a_sol corresponds to q_real but is derived from q_tsid integration.
translations.details.diagnostics.1: Confirm if joint feedback is handled by the lower-level position servo loop; separate the floating base/contact stability issue from the joint position loop.
translations.details.effective_fixes.0: A general and clean internal thread solution is to use joint torque control; position control robots typically run the TSID with virtual model states, and the CoM is modified by F/T or IMU stabilizers.
translations.details.effective_fixes.1: The user's specific machine solution does not use real floating base states, and the end-effector pose is recalibrated based on actual joint measurements, with a small bias added to the hip and ankle joints after QP.
translations.details.environments.0: TSID; Gazebo and PyBullet; position control robot; practitioners mention iCub/Talos, and the user ultimately validated on a real machine without specifying the model.
translations.details.limits.0: The maintainer explicitly states that they do not know the clean, general solution of directly feeding real states into the position control TSID.
translations.details.limits.1: End-effector error integral and joint offset are claimed hacks and cannot be directly used as general parameters for other robots.
translations.details.limits.2: Discussions on contact reference height, landing rebound, and swing/contact gain have not formed a unified rule confirmed by maintainers.
translations.details.outcomes.0: The reported solution works in simulation and real machine; no stability margin, parameter range, or cross-robot reproducibility was provided.
translations.details.problem_statements.0: Can a position-controlled robot directly compute the TSID QP using real joint/float base states, and integrate virtual states to obtain position commands?
translations.details.problem_statements.1: How can real-time deviation enter the control loop if the real state is not directly fed into the TSID?
translations.details.safety_notes.0: Before setting amplitude, speed, and integral saturation boundaries for real-world application, and before verifying in protected conditions, the original post did not provide these safety boundaries.
translations.details.suspected_causes.0: The system simultaneously enters the TSID and lower-level position controller in real-world conditions.
translations.details.suspected_causes.1: The acceleration derived from real-world state is used in a different virtual state integral, leading to inconsistency.
translations.details.symptoms.0: The system can run when only integrating virtual/command states; after calculating task error and QP with real-world state, the system diverges quickly.
translations.details.symptoms.1: Direct feedback from real-world floating base ground truth or estimator state still causes instability.
translations.details.symptoms.2: There is significant tracking error at the groin and ankle joints during the weight shift phase.
translations.media_summaries.0: The author comments include support foot reference/virtual pose curves and two landing video clips, with the text explaining the blue-green curves, reference height, and rebound phenomenon; the card does not use image or video values for supplementation, and general conclusions are only confirmed via text.
translations.source.title: Position Control Robot Directly Sending Real State to TSID Causes Double Feedback and Inconsistent State
translations.title: How do measured forces and torques, and IMU data, typically participate in stabilization when the position-controlled humanoid robot is not directly closed-loop on the real joint states within TSID?
